questions.text: Knowing that a function named fun() resides in a module named mod, and was imported using the following statement, choose the right way to invoke the fun() function:
questions.context: from mod import fun
questions.explanation: from mod import fun binds the name fun directly into the current namespace, so it's called as fun(), not mod.fun(). The mod. prefix is only needed after a plain 'import mod'.

questions.text: Assuming that the following three files: a.py, b.py, and c.py reside in the same directory, what will be the output produced after running the c.py file?
questions.context:
# file a.py
print("a", end='')

# file b.py
import a
print("b", end='')

# file c.py
print("c", end='')
import a
import b
questions.explanation: c.py prints 'c' first, then import a runs a.py for the first time (prints 'a'), then import b runs b.py, whose own 'import a' is a no-op since a is already cached in sys.modules - only b.py's own print('b') runs. Result: cab.

questions.text: Given the following Python code segment, if an exception is raised within risky_call(), how many except: blocks can be executed?
questions.context:
try:
    # Code that may raise an exception
    risky_call()
except ValueError:
    print("Caught ValueError")
except TypeError:
    print("Caught TypeError")
except Exception:
    print("Caught a different exception")
options: One or more except: blocks will be executed.
None of the except: blocks will be executed.
Exactly one except: block will be executed.
Not more than one except: block will be executed.
questions.explanation: except clauses are checked in order and at most one can match and run - execution never falls through to a second one. "Not more than one" is the precise answer because it also covers the edge case of an exception that isn't an Exception subclass (e.g. a BaseException like SystemExit), which none of these three clauses would catch at all.

questions.text: Consider the following Python code. What will be the output when this code is executed?
questions.context:
try:
    raise Exception("An error occurred")
except ValueError as ve:
    print("ValueError:", str(ve))
except BaseException as be:
    print("BaseException:", str(be))
except:
    print("Caught some other exception")
options: No output; an unhandled exception will terminate the program
questions.explanation: A plain Exception is not a ValueError, so the first clause doesn't match. It is a BaseException (Exception is a subclass of BaseException), so the second clause catches it and prints 'BaseException: An error occurred'.

questions.text: Review the Python code below. What will be the expected result when this code is executed?
questions.context:
try:
    raise Exception("An error has occurred")
except Exception:
    print("a")
except:
    print("b")
except BaseException:
    print("c")
options: The code will cause a syntax error
questions.explanation: A bare except: clause must always be the last except clause in a try statement. Here it's placed before except BaseException:, which is a SyntaxError ("default 'except:' must be last") - the code never runs at all.

questions.text: Examine the Python assertion statement provided. What is the behavior of this code segment?
questions.context: assert var > 0
options: It will raise an AssertionError if var is greater than 0.
It will do nothing regardless of the value of var.
It will raise an AssertionError if var is less than or equal to 0.
It will output the value of var if it is greater than 0.
questions.explanation: assert <condition> raises an AssertionError only when the condition evaluates to False, i.e. when var <= 0. If the condition is True, it does nothing.

questions.text: Given the Python code segment below, what is the expected behavior when this code is executed?
questions.context:
x = r"\"
print(len(x))
options: The code will print 4, as the raw string preserves the backslashes and the ending double quote is considered part of the string.
The code will print 3, as the raw string treats backslashes as literal characters.
The code will print 1, as the triple backslash in a raw string represents a single backslash.
The code will cause a syntax error due to the unescaped sequence at the end of the raw string.
questions.explanation: A raw string still cannot end in an odd number of backslashes - the backslash still escapes the following quote for parsing purposes (even though it stays literal in the value), so the string is never properly closed. This is a SyntaxError, not a valid string.

questions.text: Given the Python code segment below, what will be the output when the code is executed?
questions.context:
x = "\//"
print(len(x))
options: The code will output 3, recognizing the sequence of two backslashes as a single escaped backslash and two forward slashes.
The code will output 4, as there are four characters in the string, with the backslash escaping the following forward slash.
The code will output 2, as the double backslash represents a single backslash and the double forward slashes are combined.
The code will cause a syntax error due to an improper sequence of escape characters.
questions.explanation: \/ is not a recognized escape sequence in a regular string, so Python keeps the backslash literally (at most a deprecation-style warning, not an error). The string ends up being backslash, slash, slash - 3 characters. Verified by running it.

questions.text: Consider the Python code provided below. What will be the output of this code?
questions.context: print(chr(ord('a') + 1))
options: The code will print "a" because the addition operation does not affect the character.
The code will cause a syntax error because you cannot add a number to a character's ord() value.
The code will print "A" because the addition operation converts the lowercase 'a' to an uppercase 'A' without changing its position in the alphabet.
The code will print "b" as it takes the Unicode code point of 'a', adds 1, and converts it back to a character.
questions.explanation: ord('a') is 97, adding 1 gives 98, and chr(98) is 'b'. ord()/chr() work with plain integers, so there's no syntax error, and the result is not an uppercase conversion.

questions.text: Consider the following Python code snippet. What will be the output when this code is executed?
questions.context: print(int("1.0"))
options: The code will print 1 because it converts the string "1.0" to an integer.
The code will cause a TypeError because strings cannot be converted to integers directly when they represent a float.
The code will cause a ValueError because "1.0" is not a valid literal for the int() constructor without prior conversion to a float.
The code will print 1.0 as it maintains the floating-point format.
questions.explanation: int() only accepts strings that look like plain integers. "1.0" must first go through float("1.0") and then int(...) to succeed; passing it straight to int() raises ValueError, not TypeError.

questions.text: If the class constructor is declared in the following way, which one of the assignments is invalid?
questions.context:
class Class:
    def __init__(self, val=0):
        pass
questions.explanation: __init__ only accepts self and one optional val parameter, so passing two positional arguments (Class(1, 2)) raises a TypeError. Class(None) is fine - Python doesn't type-check val, so None is a perfectly valid value for it.

questions.text: Consider the Python class CustomNumber and the subsequent operations performed on its instance. What will be the output when the code is executed?
questions.context:
class CustomNumber:
    def __init__(self, value=1.5):
        self.value = value

    def increment(self, increase=2):
        self.value -= increase
        return self.value

num_instance = CustomNumber()
num_alias = num_instance
num_alias.increment()

print(num_instance.value)
questions.explanation: num_alias is not a copy - it's another name for the same object as num_instance. increment() subtracts increase from self.value (despite the misleading method name): 1.5 - 2 = -0.5. Since both names refer to the same object, num_instance.value is also -0.5.

questions.text: What is the expected output of the following code?
questions.context:
class A:
    A = 1
    def __init__(self):
        self.a = 0

print(hasattr(A, 'a'))
questions.explanation: hasattr(A, 'a') checks the class object A itself, not an instance. The class only carries the attribute A (capital, =1) and the __init__ method - the lowercase a attribute is only created on instances when __init__ runs, so no instance was ever made here. Attribute names are case-sensitive, so hasattr returns False. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What will the following Python code output?
questions.context:
class Parent:
    pass

class Uncle(Parent):
    pass

class Child(Uncle):
    pass

class Cousin(Parent):
    pass

print(issubclass(Child, Cousin), issubclass(Cousin, Uncle))
questions.explanation: Uncle and Cousin are sibling branches that both descend from Parent, but neither descends from the other. Child descends from Uncle, not from Cousin. So issubclass(Child, Cousin) is False and issubclass(Cousin, Uncle) is False. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What is the sys.stdout stream in Python typically associated with?
questions.explanation: sys.stdout is the standard output stream, which by default is connected to the console/screen. sys.stdin is the keyboard (standard input).

questions.text: What will be the result of running the following code?
questions.context:
class A:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.__a = v + 1

class B(A):
    def __init__(self, v):
        super().__init__(v)
        self.__a += 1

b = B(0)
print(b._A__a)
questions.explanation: Name mangling is based on the class where the code is written, not the instance's actual type. Inside A.__init__, self.__a becomes self._A__a (set to v+1=1). Inside B.__init__, self.__a becomes self._B__a - a different attribute that was never created. self.__a += 1 tries to read self._B__a first, which doesn't exist, raising AttributeError before print() is ever reached.

questions.text: What is the expected result of executing the following code?
questions.context:
def my_fun(n):
    s = '+'
    for i in range(n):
        s += s
        yield s

for x in my_fun(2):
    print(x, end='')
questions.explanation: First iteration: s doubles from '+' to '++' and yields '++'. Second iteration: s doubles from '++' to '++++' and yields '++++'. Printed back to back with no separator: '++' + '++++' = six plus signs total. Verified by running it.

questions.text: What is the expected result of executing the following code?
questions.context:
class I:
    def __init__(self):
        self.s = 'abc'
        self.i = 0

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.i == len(self.s):
            raise StopIteration
        v = self.s[self.i]
        self.i += 1
        return v

for x in I():
    print(x, end='')
questions.explanation: __next__ returns self.s[self.i], i.e. the actual characters of 'abc' at increasing indices (0, 1, 2), not the index numbers themselves. Output is the characters in order: abc.

questions.text: What will be the output of the following code?
questions.context:
def generate_pattern(n):
    def create_pattern():
        return '**' * n

    return create_pattern

pattern1 = generate_pattern(1)
pattern2 = generate_pattern(2)
print(pattern1() + pattern2())
questions.explanation: Each call to generate_pattern(n) creates a fresh closure over its own n, so pattern1() returns '**'*1 = '**' and pattern2() returns '**'*2 = '****'. Concatenated: '**' + '****' = six asterisks.

questions.explanation: readinto() reads bytes from a binary stream directly into a pre-allocated buffer (such as a bytearray) that you supply, rather than allocating and returning a new object like read() does.

questions.text: Look at the following code. Which line would you insert in order for the program to produce the expected output shown below?
questions.context:
numbers = [0, 2, 7, 9, 10]
# Insert line of code here.
print(list(foo))

Expected output: [0, 4, 49, 81, 100]
questions.explanation: FLAGGED: options 1 and 2 look malformed as transcribed (an unmatched closing parenthesis on option 1, and no wrapping call at all on option 2, which would just pack a (function, numbers) tuple) - worth double-checking their exact text against the real exam. Regardless of that, the only choice that actually transforms every element by squaring it is map(lambda num: num ** 2, numbers): map(...) applies the square to each of 0,2,7,9,10 giving 0,4,49,81,100, matching list(foo). filter(...) would instead keep/discard original elements based on truthiness of num**2 (dropping only the 0), giving [2,7,9,10] - not the expected output.

questions.text: Look at the following code. Which line would you insert in order for the program to produce the expected output shown below?
questions.context:
numbers = [i*i for i in range(5)]
# Insert line of code here.
print(foo)

Expected output: [1, 9]
questions.explanation: numbers = [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]. filter(lambda x: x % 2, numbers) keeps only the elements where x % 2 is truthy, i.e. the odd numbers themselves: 1 and 9, matching the expected [1, 9]. map(lambda x: x % 2, numbers) would instead replace each element with 0 or 1 - not what's expected. filter(lambda x: x / 2, ...) would drop only 0 (falsy) and keep everything else, giving [1, 4, 9, 16].

questions.text: Look at the code below. Which lines of code would you insert so that it is possible for the program to output the following result: 6 82 0
context:
import random

# Insert lines of code here.

print(a, b, c)

Expected output: 6 82 0
questions.explanation: randrange(10, 100, 3) can only ever produce values >= 10 that are congruent to 10 mod 3 (10, 13, ..., 97) - it can never produce 6 or 0. choice((0, 100, 3)) can only ever produce exactly 0, 100, or 3 - it can never produce 6 or 82. randint(0, 100) can produce any integer 0-100, including 6. So a=6 forces randint for a, b=82 (only achievable by randrange, since 82 = 10 + 24*3) forces randrange for b, and c=0 (only achievable by choice, since 0 is outside randrange's range) forces choice for c - exactly option C.

questions.text: What information can be read using the uname function provided by the os module? (Select two answers)
questions.explanation: os.uname() returns a structure with fields including sysname (operating system name) and machine (hardware identifier/architecture), along with nodename, release, and version. It has no concept of last login date or current path.

questions.text: What is the expected result of the following code?
questions.context:
from datetime import datetime

datetime_1 = datetime(2019, 11, 27, 11, 27, 22)
datetime_2 = datetime(2019, 11, 27, 0, 0, 0)

print(datetime_1 - datetime_2)
questions.explanation: Subtracting two datetimes gives a timedelta. timedelta's string representation only prepends an 'X day(s), ' prefix when the days component is non-zero; since the difference here is entirely within one day (days=0), it prints as plain 11:27:22 with no days prefix. Verified against Python's timedelta.__str__ behavior.

questions.text: If you want to calculate the date that is 30 days after the current date, which of the following code snippets would you use?
questions.explanation: timedelta(days=-30) and timedelta(-30) both go 30 days into the past, the wrong direction. timedelta(days-=30) is a SyntaxError - you cannot use -= inside a call argument. The credited answer is the explicit keyword form timedelta(days=30); note that timedelta(30) is functionally identical to it since days is the constructor's first positional parameter, so it also produces a correct 30-day-forward result even though it isn't the officially keyed choice.

questions.text: What is the expected result of executing the following Python code?
questions.context:
import calendar

calendar.setfirstweekday(calendar.FRIDAY)
print(calendar.weekheader(2))
options: It will only print the names of the days of the week from Friday to Sunday.
It will raise an error because calendar.weekheader() does not accept arguments.
It will print the names of all the days of the week in a shorter format.
It will only print the names of the first two days of the week starting with Friday.
questions.explanation: calendar.weekheader(n) requires an integer width argument n and returns a header with all 7 day names abbreviated to that width, ordered starting from whichever day setfirstweekday() configured (Friday here). It does not error out, and it doesn't limit the number of days shown - only their abbreviation width.
